items.title: SAI Lab Brings End-to-End Agricultural AI Workflows to Farm Science Review 2026
items.description: SAI Lab brings precision spot spraying, Smart Labeler, Intelligent Edge Management Service (IEMS), and Ask the Farm to Farm Science Review 2026, connecting field data collection, AI, high-performance computing, and agricultural decision support.
items.author: SAI Lab / NSF ICICLE AI Institute
items.body:
The SAI Lab team, participating under the umbrella of the ICICLE AI Institute, will demonstrate a set of practical AI systems for precision agriculture at Farm Science Review 2026. The team’s demonstrations connect drone imagery, AI-assisted labeling, high-performance computing, edge deployment, and geospatial decision support into workflows designed for real agricultural settings.

Farm Science Review takes place September 22–24 at the Molly Caren Agricultural Center near London, Ohio.

Precision spot spraying: From scouting to targeted treatment

The centerpiece of the SAI Lab demonstrations is a precision spot-spraying workflow that converts drone imagery into a targeted weed-treatment mission.

The workflow begins with a drone scouting plan created on a laptop. Once the drone collects field imagery, the images are automatically sent to a high-performance computing cluster for analysis. AI models perform zero-shot annotation to identify plants and weeds, and the resulting detections are assembled into a GeoPackage containing the farm boundary, detections, spray zones, and no-spray zones.

Using that spatial information, the workflow generates a waypoint-based flight plan for a spray drone. The drone can then apply treatment only in locations identified as requiring it.

This is an example of how integrated AI and computing infrastructure can support site-specific management: the system moves from image collection to geospatial analysis to an operational spray plan with minimal manual transfer between steps. By targeting treatment where weeds are detected, precision spot spraying may help reduce pesticide use and treatment costs while supporting more sustainable field operations.

Smart Labeler: Faster labels for agricultural AI

The SAI Lab will also demonstrate Smart Labeler, a system intended to make dataset labeling faster, more flexible, and easier to review.

High-quality labeled data remain a major bottleneck for building and evaluating machine-learning models. Smart Labeler enables users to label new image datasets using coordinate prompts or text prompts, then modify, filter, and analyze the generated labels. Its workflows are applicable across agriculture, ecology, and other visual-data domains.

The demonstration includes two complementary labeling modes:

  • Zero-shot labeling: Models identify objects of interest without requiring examples from the new dataset.
  • Few-shot labeling: Previously annotated images are used as ground-truth examples to guide labeling of additional images.

Smart Labeler combines multiple models across object proposal and classification stages, including SAM3, OWLv2, and DINOv3. This multi-model design is intended to support detection and classification of field-relevant objects while allowing users to inspect and improve the labels before using them downstream.

For agricultural researchers and practitioners, the practical value is clear: faster creation of curated datasets can shorten the time required to develop, adapt, or evaluate AI models for new crops, weed species, field conditions, or sensing platforms.

IEMS: Managing AI at the agricultural edge

The SAI Lab team will also show how computer-vision models can run and be managed directly at field sites through the Intelligent Edge Management Service (IEMS).

For the demonstration, a YOLO weed-detection model runs on a field-hardened NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier edge device paired with Hikrobot GigE cameras. Rather than requiring an operator to manually log into each deployed computer, IEMS manages the operational workflow from a central portal:

  • It deploys the packaged AI container and model weights to the edge device.
  • It provides access to the live camera feed.
  • It allows users to start, stop, and monitor inference from a laptop.
  • It supports management of a small fleet of in-field sensing devices.

This demonstration addresses a common challenge in agricultural AI: a model that works in the lab still needs a dependable route to deployment, monitoring, and updating in an outdoor environment. The IEMS workflow illustrates a path from a trained detector to a field-deployed application without treating every sensor box as a separate manual configuration task.

Ask the Farm: Conversational field intelligence

The fourth demonstration, Ask the Farm, provides a natural-language interface to harmonized public agricultural and environmental data.

Visitors can select a field at the Molly Caren Agricultural Center or upload their own field boundary, then ask questions about crop history, soils, rainfall, drainage, topography, and related landscape characteristics. The system is built on data layers ingested through ICICLE AI’s Earth Data Hub, including Sentinel-2 imagery, USDA crop maps, NRCS soil information, USGS hydrography and terrain layers, and rainfall data.

Ask the Farm uses open-source foundational large language models, developed with expert input and run on national academic high-performance computing resources. Importantly, the tool is designed to ground responses in the underlying geospatial information: it reports the data source, resolution, and date where applicable, and it identifies when the available records cannot answer a question.

For users, the goal is not simply to make maps easier to query. It is to make heterogeneous field-relevant information easier to discover, interpret, and connect to agricultural decision-making.

Demonstrating the full pipeline

Taken together, the SAI Lab demonstrations show a full agricultural AI pipeline:

StageDemonstrated capability
Field data collectionDrone scouting and fixed-camera sensing
Data preparationZero-shot and few-shot annotation through Smart Labeler
Scalable computingHPC-based image analysis and geospatial workflow execution
Operational actionWaypoint generation for precision spot spraying
Field deploymentEdge-based weed detection managed through IEMS
Field intelligenceConversational access to harmonized agricultural and environmental data

The team’s participation at Farm Science Review reflects a broader focus on translating AI systems research into usable agricultural workflows. Visitors will be able to see how these components connect—from collecting field data, to creating and running models, to producing field-level information and actions.

Farm Science Review 2026 is the 64th edition of the event and the 44th held at the Molly Caren Agricultural Center.

items.title: SAI Lab Showcases ICICLE-Enabled Agricultural AI at AgWireless’26 and the Farm Progress Show
items.description: SAI Lab Showcases ICICLE-Enabled Agricultural AI at AgWireless’26 and the Farm Progress Show; Brijesh Nanda B Y receives Best Poster Award for the No-Code Workflow Studio; the SAI Lab team engages farmers, researchers, and industry partners on practical AI and edge-computing challenges in agriculture.
items.author: SAI Lab / NSF ICICLE AI Institute
items.body:
The Systems and AI (SAI) Lab recently participated in AgWireless’26 and the Farm Progress Show, bringing research demonstrations in artificial intelligence, workflow automation, and edge computing to a community of agricultural producers, technology developers, researchers, and industry leaders.

The events provided a valuable opportunity to present technologies developed under the umbrella of the NSF ICICLE AI Institute and to engage directly with the people and organizations working to advance connected, data-driven agriculture. AgWireless’26 combined an ARA User Program, an NSF workshop on rural-focused NextG and agricultural innovation, and demonstrations at the Farm Progress Show; the ICICLE AI Institute was among the featured exhibitors.

Demonstrating practical agricultural AI

At the events, the SAI Lab presented two complementary technologies intended to make advanced computing capabilities more usable in agricultural environments.

No-Code Workflow Studio

Led by Brijesh Nanda B Y, the No-Code Workflow Studio enables users to design and deploy automation workflows without writing software code. The team demonstrated a precision zone-spraying workflow to show how agricultural users could configure an automated, data-informed process for a field-level application.

The work addresses a recurring barrier in the adoption of advanced agricultural technology: powerful tools often require specialized programming or systems expertise. By providing a no-code interface, the platform is designed to help domain users focus on defining their operational workflow rather than implementing its underlying software components.

Intelligent Edge Management Service

Led by Harikesh Byrandurga Gopinath, the Intelligent Edge Management Service focuses on managing edge devices and data in distributed settings. Agricultural deployments often involve heterogeneous sensors, cameras, machines, networks, and computing resources that operate far from centralized data centers. Effective management of these resources is essential for dependable field data collection, communication, and timely AI-enabled analysis.

Together, the No-Code Workflow Studio and Intelligent Edge Management Service represent complementary parts of a broader agricultural intelligence pipeline: making it easier to specify automation and supporting the reliable edge infrastructure needed to execute it.

Best Poster recognition

A highlight of the week was the recognition of Brijesh Nanda B Y’s poster, “No-Code Workflow Studio,” with the Best Poster Award.

The award recognizes the technical contribution and its potential relevance to accessible agricultural automation. It also reflects the importance of designing AI and cyberinfrastructure tools that can be used by a broad range of stakeholders—not only specialists with extensive software-development experience. AgWireless’26 included a formal poster and demo session with Best Poster and Honorable Mention awards.

Learning through collaboration

Beyond demonstrations and presentations, the SAI Lab used the events to learn from agricultural stakeholders and explore future collaborative opportunities.

Conversations with farmers, researchers, and industry participants centered on practical challenges that continue to shape the future of agricultural technology: reliable rural connectivity, integration across diverse edge devices, usable interfaces, scalable data management, and the translation of AI prototypes into systems that can support real operational decisions.

The team also participated in the ARA User Program and Arathon, which brought participants together for hands-on engagement with ARA systems and data. The experience supported the lab’s ongoing exploration of how ARA infrastructure and agricultural data may inform future digital-twin and edge-AI research directions. The ARA User Program and Arathon were core components of AgWireless’26.

Early discussions with organizations including Raptor Dynamics and Airstrike Ag also opened channels for potential future exchange and collaboration. These conversations remain exploratory, but they provide useful insight into areas of shared interest across the AgTech ecosystem.

Moving from research to impact

The SAI Lab’s participation at AgWireless’26 and the Farm Progress Show reflects a broader commitment to developing AI systems that are not only technically advanced, but also practical, accessible, and responsive to real-world conditions.

items.title: SAI Lab Undergraduates Advance to Round 2 of AISEHack 2.0
items.description: Ohio State undergraduates Amrithaa Ashok Kumar, Aarush Katta, and Maanav Jajodia advanced to Round 2 of AISEHack 2.0 in the Remote Sensing and Yield Prediction track.
items.author: SAI Lab
items.body:
Ohio State undergraduates Amrithaa Ashok Kumar, Aarush Katta, and Maanav Jajodia, who are affiliated with the Systems and AI Lab (SAI Lab) at The Ohio State University and the NSF ICICLE AI Institute, have advanced to Round 2 of AISEHack 2.0, an international AI for Science and Engineering hackathon organized by the Anusandhan National Research Foundation in collaboration with IIIT Hyderabad, GalaxEye, and IIT Madras.

Their team is competing in the Remote Sensing and Yield Prediction track, which challenges participants to develop robust AI methods for crop-pattern detection and yield prediction using remote sensing and geospatial data.

In Round 1, the team developed a crop-mapping pipeline that integrates multi-temporal X-band synthetic aperture radar imagery, agricultural masking, temporal feature extraction, and unsupervised machine learning to estimate village-level crop areas in settings with sparse and limited ground-truth data.

This work reflects the SAI Lab's broader interests in AI, cyberinfrastructure, and data-driven agriculture, while also aligning closely with ICICLE's use-inspired emphasis on digital agriculture.

AISEHack 2.0 brings together students, researchers, innovators, and AI practitioners to address real-world scientific and engineering challenges, with shortlisted teams moving on to a second online sprint and top finalists advancing to the Grand Finale in Goa, India.

items.title: SAI Lab and ICICLE Showcase AI-Enabled Agriculture Tools at Farm Science Review 2025
items.location: Molly Caren Agricultural Center, London, Ohio
items.description: Members of the SAI Lab team, part of the NSF ICICLE AI Institute, demonstrated AI-enabled digital agriculture tools at Farm Science Review 2025, highlighting practical HPC and AI workflows for on-farm decision-making.
items.author: SAI Lab
items.body:
Members of the SAI Lab team, who are also part of the NSF ICICLE AI Institute, showcased AI-enabled digital agriculture tools at Farm Science Review 2025, held September 16–18 at Ohio State's Molly Caren Agricultural Center in London, Ohio. The three-day show brings together more than 100,000 farmers, agribusiness professionals, and students to explore new technologies, management practices, and research-based recommendations from Ohio State and partners.

At the ICICLE exhibit, visitors saw how high-performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence can support practical decision-making on the farm, from crop and soil monitoring to equipment efficiency. Demonstrations highlighted how ICICLE's software components and data pipelines connect field data with AI models, enabling timely insights that can help farmers manage inputs, reduce risk, and improve profitability.

Hands-on demos included AI-powered tools for field imagery analysis, object detection, and decision support that can be integrated into existing farm operations. SAI Lab researchers—who contribute to the NSF ICICLE AI Institute—and extension specialists were on-site to answer questions, gather feedback from producers, and discuss opportunities for on-farm collaboration and testing.

By bringing these capabilities to Farm Science Review, the SAI Lab and ICICLE team aims to make advanced AI and HPC systems more accessible, interoperable, and impactful for producers of all sizes. The exhibit emphasized practical workflows that move from data collection in fields to actionable recommendations that support sustainable and resilient agricultural systems.

items.title: ICICLE Mentors High School Students for the Presidential AI Challenge
items.description: ICICLE researchers mentored high school students participating in the Presidential AI Challenge, guiding teams through problem formulation, ethical AI considerations, and solution development.
items.author: ICICLE Communications
items.body:
Researchers from the ICICLE AI Institute at The Ohio State University dedicated their time and expertise to mentoring high school students participating in the prestigious Presidential AI Challenge. Over the course of several weeks, ICICLE team members guided student teams through the end-to-end process of formulating real-world problems, designing responsible AI solutions, and presenting their work to a panel of judges.

The Presidential AI Challenge is a national competition that encourages young learners to explore the transformative potential of artificial intelligence while grappling with the ethical considerations that come with deploying these technologies. Students were tasked with identifying a problem in their community and proposing an AI-driven solution that balances innovation with fairness, transparency, and accountability.

ICICLE mentors helped students refine their ideas, navigate data collection and preprocessing, and critically evaluate the societal impacts of their proposals. The mentorship sessions also introduced students to core concepts in cyberinfrastructure, giving them a glimpse into the large-scale computing systems that power modern AI research.

"Working with these students was incredibly inspiring," said one of the ICICLE mentors. "Their creativity and eagerness to learn reminds us why outreach is such a vital part of our mission."

items.title: SAI Lab Student Presents Research at IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV)
items.description: SAI Lab graduate researcher, Satyaki Roy Chowdhury, presented posters on satellite bathymetry at WACV.
items.author: SAI Lab
items.body:
Satyaki Roy Chowdhury, a graduate researchers from the Systems and AI (SAI) Lab, presented his work at the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV 2026), held in Tucson, Arizona.

WACV is the premier international computer vision event organized jointly by the IEEE and the Computer Vision Foundation (CVF), comprising the main conference and several co-located workshops and tutorials. It is ranked among the top ten venues in the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition category according to Google Scholar's H5-index, and has consistently held a CORE ranking of A. Proceedings are published by IEEE and indexed in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library, giving accepted papers broad visibility across the global research community.

Satyaki Roy Chowdhury presented "From Bands to Depth: Understanding Bathymetry Decisions on Sentinel‑2," which examines the use of multispectral satellite data for depth estimation and improved understanding of aquatic environments.

items.title: SAI Lab Students Present Research at CSE Graduate Visit Day
items.location: The Ohio State University, CSE Department
items.description: SAI Lab graduate researchers Satyaki Roy Chowdhury and Aswathnarayanan Radhakrishnan presented posters on satellite bathymetry and geospatial AI at CSE Graduate Visit Day.
items.author: SAI Lab
items.body:
Two graduate researchers from the Systems and AI (SAI) Lab, Satyaki Roy Chowdhury and Aswathnarayanan Radhakrishnan, presented their work at the recent CSE Graduate Visit Day.

Satyaki Roy Chowdhury presented "From Bands to Depth: Understanding Bathymetry Decisions on Sentinel‑2," which examines the use of multispectral satellite data for depth estimation and improved understanding of aquatic environments.

Aswathnarayanan Radhakrishnan presented "Mining Earth's Digital Strata for Geospatial AI: Bridging Data Collection, Synthesis, and Self‑Training for Intelligent Earth Observation," focusing on advancing geospatial AI through integrated data pipelines and self-training frameworks.

Their posters reflect the SAI Lab's commitment to advancing research at the intersection of artificial intelligence, remote sensing, and Earth systems science.

items.title: SAI Lab and ICICLE Participate in An Evening of Inquiry at Columbus School for Girls
items.location: Columbus School for Girls, Columbus, Ohio
items.description: Faculty and students from the SAI Lab attended An Evening of Inquiry at the Columbus School for Girls on April 28, 2026, celebrating student-led research and K–12 engagement in AI.
items.author: SAI Lab
items.body:
Faculty and students from the Systems and AI Lab recently attended in An Evening of Inquiry at the Columbus School for Girls on April 28, 2026, an event celebrating student‑led research, creativity, and interdisciplinary exploration. This collaboration was carried out under the ambit of the ICICLE AI Institute, which supports educational outreach and K–12 engagement in artificial intelligence and computing.

The evening featured a vibrant poster session highlighting projects from participants in the Presidential AI Challenge. Several students mentored by our lab presented their work, including Caroline Lanning, Iva Karagirova, Wendy Yi, and Kendall Leff. Their projects reflected a strong engagement with emerging AI concepts and demonstrated thoughtful application of computational methods to real‑world problems, aligned with ICICLE's mission to broaden access to AI education and research.

Our lab's involvement was led by graduate student Mrunal Hole, who coordinated mentorship and research support for the school's Presidential AI Challenge participants. Mrunal worked closely with undergraduate researchers Naveen Kamath and Rishi Makineni, who assisted with guidance, project development, and preparation for the poster session, all as part of ICICLE‑supported outreach activities. Their collaboration was supported on‑site by Dr. Lisa M. Abrams, PhD, Computer Science and Math Faculty and Dean of Academics for the Upper School at Columbus School for Girls, whose leadership helped foster an inclusive and intellectually engaging environment.

The poster session provided an opportunity for meaningful dialogue between students, mentors, and attendees, reinforcing the value of mentorship and early research exposure in AI and systems. The evening concluded with a reception featuring live music and informal discussions, further strengthening connections between the school and the broader research community.

A group photograph captured the collaborative spirit of the event, featuring lead graduate student Mrunal Hole, undergraduate students Naveen Kamath and Rishi Makineni, Lisa M. Abrams, PhD, and participating students from Columbus School for Girls, all taking part under the ICICLE AI Institute's educational outreach initiative.

We are proud to support initiatives like the Presidential AI Challenge that empower young researchers and build pathways into computing and AI. Events like this reflect the growing importance of partnerships between academic research labs and K-12 institutions in shaping the future of technology and education under the umbrella of ICICLE AI Institute.

items.title: ICICLE Team Presents AI & Cyberinfrastructure at ExploreAg Technology Camp
items.description: SAI Lab / ICICLE members presented AI and cyberinfrastructure tools to high school students at ExploreAg — Ag Technology Camp, with hands-on demos of Smart Labeling, Segmentation, and Intelligent Edge Management services.
items.author: NSF ICICLE AI Institute
items.body:
Institute team members Brijesh Nanda B Y, Harikesh Byrandurga Gopinath, Qifeng Chen, Aswathnarayan Radhakrishnan and Neelima Savardekar had the privilege of presenting at the ExploreAg - Ag Technology Camp in Columbus, Ohio and represent NSF ICICLE AI Institute.

Discussed how cutting-edge technology—from precision data to automation—is actively changing the way we grow, harvest, and sustain our food supply. This was an excellent opportunity for the high school students to get their hands on ICICLE's AI & CI Service pipeline using Smart Labeling Service, Segmentation Service & Intelligent Edge Management Service to process images.

Talked all things ag tech, explored real-world applications, and looked at where the industry is heading next. Incredible energy from the students exploring how tech and STEM drive modern farming.

A huge thank you to the ExploreAg team at Ohio Farm Bureau, Ohio State University College of Food, Agricultural, and Environmental Sciences (CFAES Food, Agricultural and Biological Engineering Department) for hosting such a high-impact experience for the high school students as they look at various career pathways related to food and agriculture in Ohio.
